question: The Commission’s proposed legislation distinguishes between ‘large’ (≥ 5.6 mm calibre) and ‘small’ (< 5.6 mm calibre) centrefire bullets for hunting. However, the use of the latter for hunting is very rare in the EU, and thus practically all lead centrefire bullets would be subject to a restriction after a period of 18 months.

The UK Government is proposing a restriction based on a calibre size of above or equal to 6.17 mm, as the use of non-lead alternatives in smaller calibres may require the purchase of a new firearm or re-barrelling, given that current alternatives are either not available or not suitable.

In the EU, even that calibre size would be problematic, as it does not meet the required muzzle energy for large game in some of the Member States. That calibre size also has stabilisation issues and supply problems. In this context, it seems more logical to define the ‘large’ calibre threshold at 6.5 mm. In the light of the above: 1.
Could the Commission explain why the reasons provided by the UK Government for the exclusion of ‘small’ calibre bullets are not applicable in the EU?
Could the Commission explain whether manufacturers are able to deal with the 18month transition period, considering that around 10 % of all centrefire bullets used for hunting are non-lead?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (31.10.2025) The Commission takes note of the United Kingdom government proposal for a restriction of lead ammunition.

However, the Commission bases its proposals under the Regulation on the Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH)1 on the evidence and recommendations provided by the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) and its scientific committees, the Committee for Risks assessment (RAC) and the Committee for Socio-Economic Analysis (SEAC).
In its Annex XV restriction report2, ECHA proposed to restrict the use of large calibre (≥ 5.

6 mm) centrefire lead bullets because they found evidence that alternative non-lead bullets of those calibres (1) are readily available on the market and widely used in practice in some Member States, and (2) can be as effective as lead bullets (studies found no statistical difference in the performance of lead and non-lead ammunition of 5.56 mm calibre and higher).

ECHA proposed a transitional period of 18 months for the application of the use ban of large calibre bullets because (1) it contributes to a rapid reduction of human health impacts (IQ loss and chronic kidney disease) linked to the consumption of lead-contaminated game meat, estimated at EUR 77.

5-145 million per year; and (2) it is feasible for industry, as most ammunition manufacturers are already producing and marketing alternative ammunitions in those calibres. In their opinion3, RAC and SEAC supported ECHA’s analysis and conclusions concerning the proposed restriction measures and transitional period for large calibre bullets.
The draft proposal, including transitional periods, is currently being discussed with the Member States in comitology and their suggestions for changes will be given due consideration.
